utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom, and especially good morning, Witness. May I remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies even today. And I think Mr. Thayer has some more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you and Your Honours. Good morning to the Defence. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before we continue with the video, I'd like to follow up on the question asked by Honourable Judge Nyambe yesterday. You answered the second part of the question, I believe, but didn't get to the first part, which concerned General Mladic's repeated references, when he was getting on the buses, to Serbs being killed in the Zepa Canyon in 1992. Do you have any idea to what General Mladic was referring when he spoke about the Zepa Canyon in 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was referring to a military clash. It went this way: A column of the Serb Army, in early June 1992, set off for Zlovrh, which is one of the peaks on Mount Zepa, where the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, had had, up until then, a radio-relay and a communications centre, air control centre, and before you reached Zepa, in other words, to the west of Zepa, the Serb Army and the then organisation, they then organised people of that -- from that area. They clashed, and the column was stopped. And as far as I know, some 40 Serb soldiers were killed. When General Mladic refers to the Zepa Canyon, he is referring to these events of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge as to where these Serb soldiers who were attempting to reach the Zlovrh peak were garrisoned?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your question. I apologise. What do you mean, "garrisoned"? Perhaps I can add a few sentences; namely, I can explain what happened after this clash. The head of the column was stopped, and fighting ensued between the Serb Army and a group of people, members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, if you want. And the Serb Army had air support. At the time, there were aeroplanes over-flying the area and bombing of neighbouring villages. And after this fighting, which lasted about a day, on the next day there was a new operation where the Serb Army brought in fresh troops, and they managed to pull out the remaining Serb soldiers, so that after this incident, and this was about on the 5th or 6th of June -- after this incident, that area was peaceful, more or less. There were no major military operations there anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I ask a question to clarify just the terms. You were referring to the Serb Army and Serb soldiers. Do you mean the Bosnian Serb Army or are you referring to the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the Bosnian Serb Army, because at that time, officially, as far as I can recall, and this was in the month of June, the official presence of the JNA had already ended in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I believe that was already at the end of May. And at that time is when the change in the names occurred in the Bosnian Serb organisations, and it became the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So just to wrap up this topic, sir, were any of these Serb soldiers from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's impossible because there were only Muslims living in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Just to follow up on a couple of miscellaneous matters while we're back in time a little bit, so to speak. You testified that you left the Srebrenica area sometime in early 1993, sometime perhaps around March of 1993. Can you tell the Trial Chamber why you left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I mentioned this in my statement. In 1993, in late February, my mother passed away. She had lived in Zeleni Jadar up until then. And that was basically the main reason for my leaving there, because there was no other reason for me to stay there. The -- what prompted me also was that immediately following this, the operation against Srebrenica began. Now, I am not sure that I have all the timeline correct, but I'm referring to the events of the enclave of Srebrenica, which had shrunk at the time, and this was also the time when General Morillon came to Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was followed by attacks on Zepa. And then there was the proclamation by the UN Security Council of the protected zones, including Zepa and Srebrenica. But to go back to what I was saying earlier, my leaving Srebrenica was really directly linked to the death of my mother, because there was no reason for me to stay there and I didn't have any friends or anything like that. This was an area that wasn't really something that I was used to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And now moving back to the events of July 1995, and drawing your attention to the 19th of July, sir, would you tell the Trial Chamber why Colonel Palic did not attend the 19 July meeting with Generals Mladic and Tolimir at Boksanica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, you're talking about the talks that we all had occasion to hear about yesterday. I believe that Avdo feared for his own personal safety, and I think that's the reason why he didn't go to that meeting personally. That's as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's pick up with the video from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you have an image on your screen, sir? Do we need to get that up for you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it yet, but I'm sure I will get it in a moment. Yes, I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, again we are at 1 hour 9 minutes and 11 seconds. We just backed up the video a couple of seconds from where we left off yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see an individual in a blue shirt who's squarely facing the camera, sir? And if you do, can you tell the Trial Chamber who that person is?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's -- Peter, I believe, was his name. He was a CNN journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And directly above his head, there are three initials on the screen. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what those initials are and what they mean, if you know? It looks like a red and white and a little bit of blue colouring.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see that. That was the logo of the then Radio Television of Republika Srpska. This is in the Cyrillic script. It says there "SRT." The "se" sound looks like the Roman script C, and then "RT," so this was the Serbian Radio Television which broadcast this programme. At the time, they were in Pale. Later on, they were moved to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue playing the video, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "CNN correspondent Peter Arnett asked Hamdija Torlakovic whether the information about the alleged rapes and maltreatment in Zepa are true." "No, categorically not, definitely not. Everything going is in the best way possible, all in accordance with the signed agreement with General Mladic. The procedure is exceptionally correct, because I myself was involved in the process from the very beginning." "I'm surprised that you, as an experienced journalist of a renowned TV station, ask questions about rapes. This is Goebbels propaganda. The people are miserable. They are blaming me for rescuing Muslims and UNPROFOR members. I live for my people, for its dignity, for the honour and pride of my family and my people, and for my distinction as an officer. And I have given countless examples of this during the war." "It is 20 hours and 45 minutes. We are reporting from an area around the foothill of Zepa Mountain. The convoy with Muslim civilians, who expressed their wish to leave Zepa for Kladanj, is starting out at this moment, and it will probably be over in a few moments. The group of Muslim civilians today voluntarily left Zepa. They arrived in Kladanj in the territory under Muslim control. With the permission of the Serbian authorities, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees was escorting them. Its representatives reported, after the end, that they had crossed over." "Good evening. How are you?" "Okay, I am glad that you came, and I'm glad that CNN is present to register this, because we are helping them. No one could help them. Those who issue resolutions based on media reports only put these people in distress."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, in the footage we just saw most recently, taken at night, we saw a number of, essentially, dump trucks with people in them, and buses. Can you describe what that footage was of?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That footage was the footage of the evacuation of Zepa. The buses went directly to Kladanj, and the buses -- the trucks would stop at Boksanica, and then people would board buses and continue on their way to Kladanj. I believe that this was on the evening of the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And are those the types of trucks, for example, which you saw at Boksanica when you were there on the 26th that you spoke about in answer, in particular, to one of the honourable Presiding Judge's questions yesterday?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, these are -- this is footage from Boksanica. Now, I don't know whether at the time I was actually in any location where I could see that, but this -- these kind of convoys went on over the whole day, and this is one of the typical scenes that you could see during the evacuation of the civilian population of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: So were you still present at night-time at this location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On the night of the 26th and 27th of July, I was at check-point 2 in the UNPROFOR compound, where I spent the night in a room there. I can't recall whether Dudnjik slept in the same room, but there were a couple of UNPROFOR soldiers who slept in the same room with me. So the night of the 26th, going on the 27th, I was at this location, and I spent the night, together with UNPROFOR soldiers, in one of their dorms.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, my question about the trucks was rather more general. It was simply: Were the types of trucks that we saw in that footage, those open-back dump trucks, were those the types of trucks that you saw? Whether or not it was that exact convoy that was on the video, but were those the types of trucks that you saw arriving at Boksanica when you were there on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a frequent mention made of open-backed trucks. Yes, that was the type of truck. In other words, there was no tarp or no cover on top. But to be honest, I can't really recall every detail, whether they were yellow in colour or some other colour. I can't really recall, because this footage was made on the approaches to Zepa, at the Boksanica Plateau, and I wasn't really there at the time. I was in the UNPROFOR compound, so in an enclosed area. But I had seen such trucks earlier, and I believe that Mladic, too, mentioned that the civilian population of Zepa will be transported on these kinds of trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to the events we saw depicted on the video yesterday during the day, and I want to draw your attention particularly to the footage where General Mladic boards numerous buses and addresses the passengers. Were you aware at the time that General Mladic had a cameraman filming every time he went into one of these buses?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, when I went out, I believe that I did see a cameraman. Later on, I went to the location where we saw the footage filmed, where I was in talks with Krstic and Gvero, but I can't recall the rest. I mean, they were some 30, 40 metres away, and whether Mladic and -- the cameraman followed Mladic when he boarded each and every one of these buses, I believe so. I believe that it was the same cameraman, and I think he was a cameraman who was with the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you spent a significant amount of time over these days with General Mladic. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, based on your interaction with him, what his purpose was in getting on these buses and filming himself addressing the passengers in the way that he did?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know. I can't say either way. Thinking about it, I don't know why he would do that. Probably so that the population of Zepa could see him, get some footage of him. I don't really know. Well, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we see in the footage you drinking coffee with General Mladic. Later, you're toasting beers with Mladic, Krstic and Gvero. And were you aware that you were being filmed that entire time, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I saw the cameraman. I think he was standing to my right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were you enjoying yourself, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, it was a special situation. I know that the problem remained of the military-able men, what to do with them. Of course, it was a quite specific situation, and I was, to all intents and purposes, set aside with the Serb officers and the generals. And you must always bear that in mind when you think about my - how shall I put it? - my comments and behaviour. I was with these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How free did you feel to speak candidly about what had occurred over the prior week or so? We saw you being interviewed in the presence of that CNN reporter. Again, we saw you encircled by Mladic, his top-level generals and his bodyguards. How free did you feel to speak candidly during this time?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: Let me go back. I had to ensure -- well, what does "free" mean? I had to ensure that the process of transporting the -- transferring the civilian population would be done properly. That was our basic goal. Now, how free they felt or how free one felt to say what you wanted to say, well, everything had to be within the context of the situation, itself. And let me repeat, faced with a situation like that, quite specific circumstances, you have to understand that. Now "feel free," how can I take that? I answered what I was asked, and I had to take care and account of the situation I was in and we were in, and what our goal was at that point in time, which was for the civilian population to leave securely or, rather, to be transported to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, sir, if you could provide a little bit more detail. And I know this is not easy for you. But when you say that you had to "take care and account of the situation I was in and we were in," in deciding how to answer the questions you were being asked, for example, can you tell the Trial Chamber what exactly you were concerned about? And let me just give you an example. What do you think might have happened had you told the cameraman that civilian targets had been shelled for the last 14 days, the women and children were wounded, that the civilian population was terrified?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, if you want to get an answer, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- you shouldn't put too much details to the witness. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to greet all those present, Mr. Thayer and everybody else, and you, Mr. President. May God's will be done, and may peace reign in this house. Now, can we avoid leading questions being put to the witness, please, and not to ask for an answer from the witness on the questions being posed in the way they are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Exactly this, that was my concern. Mr. Thayer, perhaps you can rephrase or limit your question to the first part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, so I'll just make it extremely general, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What do you think would have happened had you told that cameraman what you really had experienced and were thinking and worried about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe would like to say something before the witness answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Thayer, you might want to rephrase your question. The way your question is presently phrased is speculative. "You might," "he didn't." So whatever the witness may give you may not bring out, I suspect, what you want to get out of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's now quite complicated. I would like to assist you, Mr. Thayer, if I put the question in the following way. Sir, if you recall the situation where you have been in at that time, discussing with Mr. Mladic and others, what was at that time your expectation if you would not succeed with your goal, as you explained, the safe journey of people to Kladanj, what would have happened to them? What did you have in mind at that time when you were sitting there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this: If the population had not been moved to Kladanj in this way, then it would have had to have stayed -- they would have had to have stayed on the mountain, those people. Now, what would have happened next is a matter of speculation. But, at any rate, it would have been an incomparably more difficult situation for survival, in terms of survival, than the other one. Now, linked to the Prosecutor's question about what would have happened had I said, Yes, such and such, such and such, my answer is I don't know what would have happened, of course. But it's a hypothetical question. And let me repeat, once again, that situation, and not only that one, you have situations like that in life, when you follow your goal and purpose, and it doesn't enter your mind to question things. Now, what would have happened had I told the CNN journalist that, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The footage, sir, for example, where we see General Mladic telling you about honour, his officers' distinction, and referring to Goebbels propaganda and so forth, you were there at the time when he was saying these things to you, and you've seen the footage. How would you characterise what General Mladic was doing during this interaction with you, when he's on one side with his officers and you're alone on the other side in the chair in front of the cameras? How would you characterise that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't think about an answer to a question like that, and now I'm giving thought to it. But you can assume what the situation was like, and I was helpless. I can say that now. I had to do this, that. And, well, let me repeat. The situation was what it was. I was alone up there. You have General Mladic in front of you, with his military leaders around him. You have the transport of the population. My role, if I can put it that way, and everything I did had to be such that the process was brought to an end, was completed. It would be strange of me to say anything else, except to say, What could you have been? You had to be courageous to say it wasn't this way or that way. That would have required courage. And that was my third meeting, I believe, with General Mladic. I already knew what his behaviour was like, and what his story was, and what his relationship was towards his subordinates, how he acted towards them and others. So what can I say? It was a very difficult situation for me to be in. But on that day, and as the day went on, when I said "relaxing," I meant that there were other topics discussed, too, when there wasn't any filming going on. As I say, that's how it was. I don't think I need describe it anymore. Anybody looking at it and looking at the situation, and anybody aware of what the situation was like, would be able to draw their own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Thayer, everybody in the courtroom, both parties and the Chamber, at the end, will draw conclusions of what we have seen and what the witness described. I think it's not essential to ask him about his conclusions. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you carry on, Judge Nyambe would like to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 13, lines 16 to 17, just now you have said: "And that was my third meeting, I believe, with General Mladic." My question is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fourth. I made a mistake. I made a mistake. It was the fourth meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. My question is: This being the fourth meeting, and in all these meetings you have observed the conduct of General Mladic, as you say, his relations with his subordinates, his relations with other people in these meetings, did you feel at any time that after attending maybe one or two meetings that you wouldn't want to attend another meetings with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when I said that I saw what his conduct was, Mladic's conduct was, towards his subordinates, I want to say that General Mladic was always the number-one man in any situation. He was all -- he always had the main say, and nobody would oppose him in any way. They just answered his questions. Now, his relationship towards others, his conduct towards others, would change depending on the situation, going from cold to warm to hot. Now, as far as I'm concerned, I entered into this process, I did not have any -- how shall I put this? I didn't -- it didn't enter my head not to go -- not to attend a future meeting, whatever happened. And I've already said that, I believe, in my testimony, that Mr. Benjamin gave up on the meeting of the 24th of July, so that I arrived at the meeting alone. Mr. Benjamin did not come because the stakes were high. What had to be assured was the safe departure of the civilians from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's talk about the events of the 27th of July for a few moments. You told us yesterday, in connection with some of the questions from the Trial Chamber, that you remained at Boksanica until sometime on the 27th. Can you tell the Trial Chamber approximately what time of the day it was when the last convoy which you saw arrive at Boksanica was?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was several hours after noon, sometime in the afternoon, maybe 1.00 p.m., 2.00 p.m., and the convoy was stopped at Boksanica. Everybody stopped there. And from the convoy -- well, I was in the UNPROFOR compound, myself, at the time, but Mehmed Hajric and Amir Imamovic came or were brought, and we were together -- there together. And when I asked how come they were there, they had come, I think the answer was that they stayed until the end to draw up lists of the people who were boarding the buses. The situation changed at that point, and as far as I can remember, we were told that the convoy would not be going any further until the fighters and military-able population had surrendered. Now, the president of the Wartime Presidency was there at the time. His name was Mehmed Hajric. And so most of the pressure was on him. And I think that the piece of paper which I've forgotten now, but which was shown me during the proofing session on Sunday for my testimony, I think this piece of paper was signed by Hajric, myself, and Imamovic, and that, again, was agreement for the army to surrender. I think I told General Mladic once again that that piece of paper cannot be effective because nobody could wield influence of that kind on anybody else to prevail upon them to come in and surrender. Now, following on from my memories of the situation, Mehmed Hajric was sent to Mount Zepa to convey the demands or to describe the situation and the demand for the army to surrender. I think he went off from Boksanica in an UNPROFOR vehicle, and the rest of us stayed behind; that is to say, I and Amir Imamovic stayed behind. So that might have been 3.00 in the afternoon by that time on the 27th of July. An hour or two later, I was sent to one of the buses from the convoy, the last convoy arriving from Zepa, which was parked at Boksanica. I went into one and Amir Imamovic went into another, so we weren't together. We went into separate buses. Now, time passed with nothing happening, but then, as far as I recall, at around 9.00 or 10.00 in the evening of the 27th of July, that soldier -- the Serb soldier arrived and told me to follow him. I saw that another soldier was taking Amir out from this other bus, the one he was in. Then we were taken to the area where I had slept in the UNPROFOR compound. Along the way, we heard that on the stretch from the bus to that UNPROFOR compound, that instructions were given for the convoy to continue on its way to Kladanj. I heard the engines being switched on and the buses setting off. After some time had gone by in this UNPROFOR compound, I think two men entered. They might have been the military police of the Army of Republika Srpska. And Amir and I were told that we were arrested, under arrest, and that we now had the status of prisoners of war. They put handcuffs on our hands. Well, they joined our hands with the handcuffs, one of my hands and one of Amir's, and ordered us to follow them. We left the area, the UNPROFOR compound. And let me just say that while we were being arrested, there were a couple of UNPROFOR soldiers standing by and Colonel Dudnjik, who turned the other way. When we left, we took the forest route, and later on I realised why this was done. Anyway, that part of the road, that stretch of the route, some 100 metres, was through the woods, and we joined up onto the road later on after that, and we entered a vehicle that was familiar to me. And I think it's one that was used by the Army of Republika Srpska, some sort of APC. They put us in, and we were driven off to the hotel at Borike, where we were taken over by some young guys. Well, I think they were also from the military police of the Army of Republika Srpska. We spent the night, and they stood guard over us. We spent the night there, which was the 27th -- between the 27th and 28th of July. In the morning, they unlocked our handcuffs, gave us some breakfast, and sent us back to Boksanica in a vehicle of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I might just interrupt you, sir, for a moment. So just based on your last answer, did you spend the night in the room handcuffed -- still handcuffed to Mr. Imamovic, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that clearly from my answer. We were handcuffed, let's say, at around 11.00 p.m., and the handcuffs were taken off in the morning at 7.00 a.m. So 11.00 p.m. of the 27th, and we spent the night. Well, we sort of slept. And on the morning of the 28th, at about 8.00, they took our handcuffs off, gave us some breakfast, and we set out for Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I think you told us that the situation became tense on the 27th. Did General Mladic's attitude change that day as well in any way?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 27th? Well, yes, the situation, up until the arrival of the last convoy, was quite different, more relaxed. But when the last convoy arrived, then the whole mood changed. General Mladic asked the army to surrender. He asked me first. And then the president of the Wartime Presidency, Amir Imamovic, was there. So that was at around 2.00 in the afternoon of the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you say that the whole mood changed, did General Mladic's mood change in any way?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. "Mood," you use the word "mood," but, in fact, it's the position that he took. Now, it was said, Okay, we have an agreement signed and now the army has to surrender. And I told General Mladic that -- while I was signing that agreement, that I had no competence, no authority, or no effective control over the army, and that was the substance of our conversation, more or less. Now, Mehmed Hajric was present as well, and I believe then the conversation moved to -- he started talking with him, that perhaps he should -- because he was -- he should inform a member of the Presidency. But, generally, I know that the whole relationship -- the whole treatment changed, but I don't know what caused it and it would just be my guessing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to signing the agreement, which agreement are you referring to? Because the Trial Chamber has heard reference now to a number of meetings and agreements, so just so that there is no lack of clarity on the record, what agreement or document are you referring to now?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was referring to the only agreement that we were shown yesterday. That was the agreement on disarming the soldiers of Zepa. That was the agreement I was referring to, the agreement of the 24th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on the 27th of July, this day we've been spending some time on now, did you sign -- and I think you've already spoken a little bit about this, but just so the record is clear, did you sign another document? And I'll just leave it there for now.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The signing of that document followed the discussion, and that is the document that I said I had seen it for the first time on Sunday, during the proofing session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you saw that agreement on Sunday, did you recognise anyone's signature on it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised my own signature, although there were three there, Mehmed Hajric's, mine, and Amir Imamovic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how, if at all, did seeing that agreement jog your memory about the events of the 27th?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all I can say about the agreement is that it was the result of pressure exerted on the three of us to surrender the Zepa -- the soldiers of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you say "pressure," sir, what are you referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation was as follows: The last convoy had been intercepted, and they said that the convoy would not continue on its way until the army surrendered. That's the pressure that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to show you a document shortly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just want to let the Trial Chamber know one thing about it. This was seized during some searches a few months ago. The document will be the subject of a 65 ter motion to add it to our exhibit list. If the Trial Chamber wishes not to use the document at this point, that's fine. We have at least one other witness through whom the document may be used. I have asked the Defence if there is any objection to using the document, subject to a future Rule 65 ter addition motion. We do have one in the works, some pleasure is yet to come for the Trial Chamber. But I just wanted to alert the Trial Chamber to that fact, that this is a document that we did not have at the time the witness testified the last time, as the Trial Chamber has heard from the witness, and it was shown to him during the proofing session. So I just notify the Court of that. And should the Court permit, I would like to show the document to the witness. Otherwise, I think there's a sufficient foundation laid and we can use it with another witness at another time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you tell me, is this the 65 ter number 06418?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. And it was after the proofing, frankly, that I realised that it was not part of our 65 ter list, that it was part of the motion that is in the works. And rather than burdening the Trial Chamber with yet another motion, because I know we had a few in the pipeline already, as I said, we're certainly flexible on whether to use it or not with this witness. It's entirely up to the Trial Chamber's preference, whether you want to wait for the formal motion to add it to the 65 ter list before using it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you able to respond to this proposal by Mr. Thayer? What is your position about using this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, but I am not really sure what document they mean. Perhaps they could tell us something about the content of that document, because I don't know what Mr. Thayer might be referring to here. And I don't really have any objections to everything being actually publicised, but we don't know anything about the earlier document that was mentioned here either, and there was no mention made about whether the agreement was complied with or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last document we have received yesterday or even the day before - I don't recall - was on the 65 ter list, and we saw it on the screen, and you have received it earlier. This document, we don't -- as a Chamber, don't know anything about it, except that it is listed in the list of documents the Prosecution was intending to use. Mr. Thayer, would you explain a little bit further, for the sake of Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. And just so the Trial Chamber is aware, this is a document that has been previously disclosed. I advised the Defence almost, I think, a week ago that I was intending to show this to the witness and that we might be using it as an exhibit in court. This is a document that was seized during the course of some searches related to ongoing investigations. It is part of a collection of search-related documents which are still being processed and analysed, so even the attorneys don't have the full scope yet of what is being produced from this cache of documents found during the search. But this one was brought to my attention recently. And as soon as it was and I realised its importance, we notified the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To clarify the situation, you have asked the witness about a certain agreement again, and he referred to that we have seen yesterday on the screen. This is the agreement of the 24th of July with the signature of this witness. But recently, today, the witness mentioned another agreement with a signature of Mehmed Hajric and Amir Imamovic and his own signature, and this seems to be the agreement you are referring to now with the 65 ter number 06418, is that correct, with the date of the 27th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we do not object to any of the documents that was signed by the Army of Republika Srpska and by this witness being made public, but we do object to documents being used which we know nothing about, because I saw yesterday a number of matters that actually do not correspond to what was happening. For instance, there was some footage showing me in civilian clothes, and there was no mention made where that was filmed or what it was about, and similar matters. So that's all I would have to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the moment, we are only discussing this agreement, this document with the number -- 65 ter number 6418. You say you are not objecting to this, and Mr. Thayer told us that it was disclosed to you and to the Defence. If that is the case, then you are aware of this document and the content or not? I don't understand your comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my comment is this: If the witness is asked about something that we can only guess about, then I can't really agree to that. But if there is an agreement that was signed by this witness and by the Republika Srpska Army, I absolutely have no objection to it being shown here in the courtroom and then questions being asked about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, Witness, may I ask: Are you the only person still alive from the Bosnian community who signed this agreement we are talking about of the 27th of July? Are you the only person still alive of the Muslim community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you are moving for admission of this document to the 65 ter list, and taking into account that there is no objection by the Defence, by Mr. Tolimir, for using this document, your motion is granted without a written submission, and you may use it now by examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And just to keep things a little smoother, I hope, we may as well just do this in private session, rather than trying to blow up certain sections and jump in and out. If we can just go into private session to look at the document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you've been testifying about numerous events, going back to 1992. And as you just said, you've told us on a number of occasions about the fear. And in your last answer, you just said: "Whether that was founded or not, that's a different issue." Well, I'm asking you: Was it a founded fear -- was it a well-founded fear or was it not a well-founded fear in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, indeed, that is probably a question that you shouldn't put to me, in other words, what would have happened had the army surrendered -- had the troops surrendered. I've already said that I don't know what would have happened, but that that was the reason why they didn't surrender. Now, I wouldn't want to speculate, so my answer would be this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I see we're at the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must have the first break now. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And just to let the Trial Chamber know, we are rounding the bend. I think maybe another half an hour. We're going to look at some maps and do some markings, and we'll see how that goes, but we're reaching the end of the sort of chronological --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you move to that topic, I have one question to the agreement we have seen. It was called "Agreement," but the headline was "Decision," and the text supposes that it was a decision by the War Presidency. But was it discussed among you, the members of the War Presidency, or was it just given to you as a draft from the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, that's what we received from the Serb side. And a correct translation of the word "odluka" is "decision."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 06418 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P736.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: By this time on the 27th of July, sir, can you describe for the Trial Chamber, without necessarily going into all the specifics, but can you describe the nature and the frequency of your contacts with the BiH authorities in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- an additional question for me. For what period? The 13th of July to the 27th of July, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's focus, say, from the 20th of July to the -- or the 25th of July to the 27th of July. I think you've already told us about the steps that you took after your meeting on the 13th, and again after your meeting on the 19th, and again after your meeting on the 24th. But by this time, on the 27th, say from the 25th of July, what kind of contacts had you had with Sarajevo, and to what degree were you acting and making decisions in consultation with them or not in consultation with them?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: After the agreement was signed on the 19th of July, 1995, I remember that we -- or, rather, my first contact, if I can put it that way, or, rather, contact with the political leaders in Sarajevo, which I attended in Zepa, was in the evening of the 19th; the night between the 19th and 20th of July, in fact. And I think that there was some discussion and talks with Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, who was president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. And as far as I recall, everything boiled down to the fact that the civilians -- attempts should be made to pull the civilians out, the women and children. As for the army, we appealed at the time that they try to reach an agreement with the Serb side on an "all for all" basis at a higher level. And that's mostly how -- what the outcome of those contacts were. And they said the following day in Sarajevo, there would be an initiative launched via UNPROFOR to contact the Serb side. Now, the next contact was, as far as I remember, on the 24th of July, in the evening once again, and we were informed -- or, rather, we informed Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, I think it was, of the fact that Zepa had, in fact, fallen, in military terms, and that an agreement had been signed with the Serb side so that the evacuation of the civilians would go ahead in the coming days. I can't remember all the details now. I might have had an occasion to look at some documents which -- this conversation between the War Presidency of Zepa, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic -- anyway, other contacts where I sat on the other side in Zepa, they weren't audio conversations; they were protected lines, protected communication. The text would be typed out, and feedback or an answer to that text would appear on the screen. So I didn't take part in any further negotiations and talks. And in view of the location of the devices used by the army for this purpose, it was a relatively long distance away and you needed time to reach this location on Mount Zepa. And that was difficult, so you couldn't go there in 15 minutes. You needed an hour or more. Anyway, that device was one which the army used, so that all the information coming in from anybody, whether from the military or from the political leaders in Sarajevo, reached that location, and that information was read -- the incoming information was read by the army first, army members in charge of manning the device, and then later on probably forwarded to Colonel Palic or one of his officers. The last thing I remember is that we informed Sarajevo that Zepa had, in fact, fallen, in military terms, to all intents and purposes, and that the evacuation of the civilians would start the very next day, that is to say, on the 25th. And I think we launched another appeal for them to find ways and means of ensuring that the able-bodied men in Zepa be exchanged for all the imprisoned Serb soldiers, an "all for all" -- on an "all for all" basis, and I think the response was that they would try to do something about that. So that's what I can tell you about the contacts with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to clarify one matter. In your answer, sir, you refer to an agreement being signed on the 19th of July. Was there, in fact, any agreement signed on the 19th of July?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's my mistake. It's not the agreement that was signed, just the conditions that we were given by the Serb side were conveyed and forwarded. So no written agreement was signed or any piece of paper. That's my mistake. I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You also told us that in one of the conversations with Sarajevo, you were told that there would be some type of meeting or meetings to be held at the airport in Sarajevo. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I think it was the last contact that I had or the conversation I attended with the sides -- the parties in Zepa, and that was the 24th, the night between the 24th and the 25th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to what extent, if any, did you, yourself, or your fellow members of the Zepa War Presidency become aware, during this period of time, that with respect to trying to reach an "all for all" prisoner exchange agreement in Sarajevo, the issue of men from -- unaccounted men from Srebrenica had arisen? To what extent, if any, were you made aware of those developments in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me, personally, I wasn't, because I think Colonel Palic had most information because the papers reached him directly, I assume. But I wasn't informed about that, or at least I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You told us that you recall meeting General Smith on the 25th of July. Do you recall meeting General Smith at any other time again during these three days, meaning the 25th, 26th, 27th of July?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting with General Smith, well, I can't locate it -- pin-point it exactly, whether it was the 26th or the 27th, but one of those two days, and I remember it for the following reasons: I don't know how I received the information that Colonel Palic gave me, saying that at the meeting in Sarajevo at the airport, that an exchange had been agreed upon of the able-bodied men of Zepa for the captured Serb soldiers and that it was a done deal, so to speak. And I was told that I would be informed about that further by General Rupert Smith at the meeting which Sarajevo said would take place at Boksanica. Now, when he arrived at the beginning of the meeting, I was fairly relaxed at that point, and I think that I broached the subject first and told General Rupert Smith about it. And General Rupert Smith was the commander, let me explain, of UNPROFOR for Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. However, I conveyed this information, that everything had been agreed upon over there, but I remember very well that General Rupert Smith nodded or, rather, said, No. He made this negative sign with his head, said nothing had been agreed upon, and he started looking back through his note-book, confirming that a meeting had, indeed, taken place at the airport between the representatives of the political leaders of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Serb side. Anyway, he shook his head and said that nothing had been finalised. And this was like a cold shower, as far as I was concerned. That meeting might have been either on the 26th or 27th. I can't be quite sure. I can't confirm whether it was on the 26th or the 27th, but it was at check-point 2 at Boksanica. UNPROFOR's check-point 2, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You told us that you were seized by VRS soldiers, whom you believed were military police, in the presence of UNPROFOR, including Colonel Dudnjik. Were you able to form any impressions, based on your time in Boksanica and down in the center of Zepa, of these Ukrainian peacekeepers?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw -- or, rather, from what I saw and in the brief contacts that I had with Colonel Dudnjik, the composition of the Ukrainian Battalion at the time in Zepa was -- in my opinion, they were a collection of frightened young men who happened to find themselves in this predicament, in this situation, so that they were not able to do anything significant. And as far as I remember -- I don't know if I've said this already, but, anyway, on one occasion I remember talking, through a radio-relay connection from Zepa, to a French general or colonel who was at the time the commander of UNPROFOR for the Sarajevo region or something like that, asking for assistance for us, and he said he was just worried about the UNPROFOR soldiers' security and safety. And as to all the rest, he said that that was up to the politicians to find a political solution. So those are my impressions about these UNPROFOR soldiers and their attitude to the situation that they found themselves in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were you able to observe or did you have any information about how well supplied or well provisioned these peacekeepers were in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, during that period they had a problem with basic supplies; fuel, for instance. I don't know if they had enough food, but I know that fuel was always a problem. And so when I went there a couple of times using one of their vehicles, we always had to stop off and tank up from another vehicle. So I think that during that period, they didn't have enough fuel supplies to function properly. Now, as to food and cigarettes, I can't say. I don't know. But I do know there was a fuel shortage.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you were seized by these VRS soldiers and taken away with Mr. Imamovic in front of their eyes, did any of those peacekeepers try to intervene in any way?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I think that Colonel Dudnjik turned his head away, faced the other direction, not to have to look at all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That brings us to the 28th of July, sir. You told us that in the morning, you were un-handcuffed from Mr. Imamovic, given breakfast, taken to Boksanica. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were taken to Boksanica again. I don't know what vehicle it was. I think it belonged to the Army of Republika Srpska. And we were escorted there by those two military policemen belonging to the Army of Republika Srpska. We sat to one side, and I saw General Mladic there again passing by. He passed by me. He didn't greet me at all. And as far as I remember, I was called in for an interview. I was questioned by, I think, a security officer of the Republika Srpska Army. I don't remember his name or what he looked like, actually, but he asked for general information first. The questioning went on for a brief period, maybe 20 minutes at the outset. I don't know if we talked about anything else. But, anyway, General Mladic then called the officer to him and said they were going. And I remained there. After that, the military police, I think it was, of the VRS took myself and Imamovic back to the hotel at Borik, and I think they separated us on that occasion and put us into two different rooms. We spent about three days there, two or three days, as far as I remember. And after that, we were taken out of our rooms, and I saw that Mr. Mehmed Hajric was there. He was the third man. I didn't know previously that he was also there. Anyway, they transported us in a civilian car, a Volkswagen Golf, I believe. They took us from the hotel at Borike to the prison in Rogatica, and I think that was the 30th of July, 1995. We were put up there in a separate facility, myself, Mehmed Hajric and Imamovic. Well, it was a prison, as I learnt later, which had another 40 elderly persons and wounded incarcerated there, men who were part of the last convoy held back at Boksanica. And as I already stated, it was the following day when we were brought there, the next day in the morning. An International Red Cross team arrived and registered us, and that's when we were given those cards and numbers and the possibility of sending messages to our families and friends. Some 15 days later, as I've already said, Amir Imamovic and Mehmed Hajric were taken off, not to return to the premises that I was in. During my time in prison, I worked as an electrician with the electrical installations and new facilities at Borike, and I spent about a month and a half at Borike, in fact. After some time, I think perhaps two months later, representatives of the International Red Cross came to visit us again and brought what we needed for personal hygiene, and some clothing, and things like that. And at the beginning of January, we were transferred first to Kula, which is a prison near Sarajevo, which was controlled by the Serb side, and we spent three or four days there waiting for an exchange of some kind. And then I think it was on the 15th of January, 1996, that we were exchanged according to the Dayton Accords. I arrived in Sarajevo. So that would be it. That was my journey and how I reached Sarajevo from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back for a couple of follow-up questions. When you were being held at that hotel in Borike over the three-or-so-day period before you were taken to the prison, were you under guard? And if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was always one member of the Army of Republika Srpska. I think they were military police. In every room there were guards, and we even exchanged words. We talked about events and developments. And if I can put it that way, we were on friendly terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with respect to the prison, can you describe, just generally for the Trial Chamber, where it was located?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the prison was relatively close to the main road. It was in Rogatica, which is a town in Eastern Bosnia to the south of Zepa. And I had never been in Rogatica before, so that I didn't really know it well. It was a small town, and the prison was on the premises of what had been some kind of farm earlier. And the administrative building was -- the prison, itself, was in the administration building of that farm. It was close to the main road leading to Sokolac, at the foot of Mount Romanija. Let's say it was in the western part of Rogatica. It was a one-storey building. There were no other floors, so it was only a one-level building.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you remember specific names, that's fine, but I'm more generally interested in who was in charge of the prison. Who ran the prison? Was it civilian police, MUP, VRS?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was run by the Army of Republika Srpska, because there was also a detention area, not where we were, but in a different facility, where there were also members of the Army of Republika Srpska who were detained there for two or three days, a sort of military prison, and the prison, itself, was run by the Army of Republika Srpska. And I think that the warden or prison commander was -- I can't really recall the name right now, but you can find that out maybe from some other witnesses. In any case, the security was provided by the military police of Republika Srpska Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you mentioned being taken down to Zepa centre as part of your work as a prisoner, and that that's when you saw the destroyed mosque and torched homes. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber when that was, approximately? Even just a month, if that's all you remember.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably in November, approximately. It's very likely that it was November, November of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we go into private session for one question, Mr. President, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that will be page 13 in e-court. And if anybody has their hard copy map books handy, it's page 11 of the actual map book.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, do you have an image on your screen? And I appreciate, if you do, it's probably hard to read.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- if we can blow up the section -- if we see where it says "65th Protection Regiment base." If we start at the word "base" and blow up a section of those two squares on the map below and to the right. Sorry, keep going. That's perfect, perfect, perfect, perfect, perfect. Okay, stop, please, and let's see if we can -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, Mr. Thayer, could you -- I know that, but could you please repeat what it is about, what we are seeing, and which kind of map it is, and who did the markings?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This is P104. It is a map from the map book. The map is a VRS map that was obtained by the OTP. The sections in white blocks -- rectangular blocks were added by the OTP, but all the other markings are from the original map. And I should add, if we look at the key, there are some items that are circled. And as the key explains, obviously those little circles were also added by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you referred earlier in your testimony to a number of villages which were cleansed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we can move the image slightly to the left. Keep going. We'll see how much we can catch. Keep going all the way. More. Okay, and up a little bit. Okay, perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you simply to mark with a number a couple of the locations that you told us about earlier in your testimony, and I'll ask you to do that with this little stylus that will -- there we go. Do you see the location of Podzeplje on the map? And if you do, could you mark it with the number 1?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's fine. I think we've lost part of the name on the map, itself. I think part of the actual name is still visible. But can you identify the general location, if you don't see the full name, of Rijeka? And just put a number 2 where --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just a moment. Where do you want me to put it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: As close to where you would identify Rijeka as being.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it's "Rijeke," with an E at the end. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My apologies to your language. And can you place the number 3 at the location of Godjenje?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps if you can scroll it up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's not possible to move it anymore because we will lose your previous markings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Well, it's not really necessary. It's quite all right. A "3"?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you referred to the location of Brloznik earlier in your testimony. Can you place a 4 next to that location, please?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also referred to the village of Borak. If you can locate that and place a number 5, that would be helpful as well, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I think we've got everything. If we could save it. I don't know what the Chamber's preference is, whether to have the witness initial it or not or whether it's sufficient just to save it at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You're tendering this document as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We will tender it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, and no marking -- additional marking necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The marked map will be Exhibit P737.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you referred in your testimony to the confrontation line more or less running along a series of villages that included Godjenje and some others. In July of 1995, during the course of the VRS attack on Zepa, did you become aware that defensive positions were set up on the northern side of the enclave? I believe you told us that there was a defence line set up at the southern side facing Boksanica and that there were VRS attacks from the area of Godjenje. Were there a defence line or were there positions taken at any locations that you're aware of on the northern side of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know much about that, but it would be logical to cover some points in the northern part of the enclave, from -- in the area where an attack was expected from; for instance, the Brloska Planina. Then Stublic would have been another location to set them up at because you could reach the enclave going -- taking that road. I don't know any others, but it would have been logical to do that, to cover some of these points in the northern part. And Colonel Palic was involved in this. And I know that I talked to some soldiers later on who had been at the Prlog Mountain during the attack of the Serb Army on Zepa, and from what they told me, I know that that area was shelled and there were also infantry attacks, but I don't know exactly when Brezova Ravni [as interpreted] fell, where exactly the lines ran. I really don't know, because it was only six months later that I actually learned about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's scroll slowly to the right, please, and see if we can see some of these locations which you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is still P104?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President. Yes, that's what we have on the screen. Keep going and stop. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Again, we're looking at the same map as we looked at a moment ago, P104. You, I think, just referred to a location, Brloska Planina. If you can place a number 1, if you can find that and tell us what that actually is. Does "planina" mean anything, does that word anything, and what kind of a feature or area is it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "planina" would be in English -- Brloska Planina is a toponym and it's a mountain. And there are some villages at the bottom, Brloznik, and that's where the name, Brloska Planina or Mountain came from. So it is a mountain, it's an elevation. It has an altitude of over 1200 metres. And from Brloznik to the plateau on the mountain, you have to pass a very steep road to reach that plateau. I don't know what else to say. Would you like me to put number 1 there?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Please, sir.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You also mentioned a location by the name of Stublic. And if you would place the number 2 next to that location, if you can locate it on this map, and explain why that made a logical defensive position.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Let me find Stublic. Here it is, and I'm putting number 2 there [marks]. And you can even see on this map that in order to get to Stublic, coming from the north, you would take a road. This was not an asphalt road. It was actually a path through the woods, but it was passable. And this is where the axis of the Serb Army could have been. They could bring their supplies in using this road. So this is the road that could be used to reach the northern parts of the Zepa enclave, and that is why Stublic was very important as a defence feature, because once you reached the Zepa Mountain, then it was a fait accompli for Zepa. And even if these positions, Brezova Ravan and others to the south, were completely protected, you would still have lost that area. So Stublic was a very significant defensive position.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in between these two locations you've marked as number 1 and number 2, we see an area called "Radava" both in big letters and then a smaller "Radava" underneath that. I don't know if you can see that, sir. It's roughly in between the two numbers you've marked, "Radava." Have you been able to locate that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've located them both.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge as to whether there was any military significance to this area known as Radava?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a familiar area, because I actually went through this area in the summer of 1992. Below Mount Brloznik, there was a plateau called Radava, and it was possible to reach Radava. You can't see it here on this map, but there was a road leading from Kupusna. I believe that was the name. So this was another road that could be used by an army. So Radava, too, was significant. That is the road that you can see right next to the letter R of the small letters "Radava." I think that's the road. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just for the record, you've drawn a squiggly line emanating from the capital R of "Radava" going upwards to the left. If you could just mark a number 3 next to this location, Radava, so we can refer to it later on when we review the record, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. We're done with this set of markings. If we could save it, and the Prosecution would now tender this exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P738.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just one last set of questions on this map. Again, we're going to stick with P104. If we could just scroll down a little bit, please. A little bit more. A little bit more. A little bit more. Okay, perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Throughout your testimony, you referred to Zepa Mountain, and you've also referred to a feature of that mountain by the name of Zlovrh.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zlovrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. First, can you write a number 1, please, next to "Zlovrh"?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you referred to the portion of the civilian population fleeing from the southern part of the enclave to Mount Zepa, can you perhaps draw a square or some kind of shape which captures the general area that you were talking about where these civilians were congregating when they left their homes for Zepa Mountain?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] Roughly here, the broader area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you could place a number 2 inside that rough circle, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see here that the area you've indicated lies within a portion of the map marked "Sjemec." If you could perhaps underline the word "Sjemec" for us, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to underline the name "Sjemec"; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, but what do you want me to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just underline it, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, was "Sjemec" a term that people from Zepa used to refer to this location?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time that I see this "Sjemec." I never heard it used in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now, you referred to the location of Stitkov Dol. If you could locate that, please, and write a number 3 next to it.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. And, finally, you referred to the Zepa River during your testimony. It might be a little hard to see, but if you could locate that and just draw a line underneath where you can see the Zepa River so it's easier for us to see and locate.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Witness. And if you would, please, just place a number 4 next to that marking. Anywhere you like next to that marking.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We're done with this map now. We can save it, and Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P739.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with that, I thank you, Witness. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thayer. You have several times indicated the time you would use. It was longer and longer. We were very patient with you, but I think it was very important to receive this evidence of the witness. Mr. Tolimir, would that be a convenient time to commence your cross-examination or would you like to have the second break now in order to prepare your cross-examination? Perhaps, for the witness it's better to have now a half-hour break and then commence the cross-examination. It's a question to you and for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. As far as I'm concerned, we can start straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If that is the wish of the witness, we can do that. I abide by your ruling and his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, you have the floor and you should start with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to officially greet the witness now, because we're going to have our communication now. I wish him a pleasant stay and would like to emphasise that if there's anything he needs, whether he wants us to proceed more slowly or whatever, we can do that and switch topics that are not as taxing. But we're going to continue the discussion of the subject that was discussed, the location of Zepa, the corridors between Zepa and Srebrenica, and I don't think that's a difficult topic. And for us to do that, let's have the map back up on our screens, please, document P504, it was, Prosecution document 504.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So while we're waiting for the map to come up --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or, rather, may I have P504 called up on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you asking for 504 or 104? The last map was P104.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P04, because that's the whole map -- the map book together and the Drina Corps, a close-up. It's P107, in actual fact, P107. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And at this point in time, I would like to ask both speakers not to overlap. Because you are using the same language, you should pause between question and answer and question, for the sake of the record and the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It was my fault.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we zoom in, please, so that the witness can see the place names better, "Srebrenica" and "Zepa." Thank you. We can see the Zepa locality here. That's right, that's fine, because now we can see both Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, Witness, please, could you tell us precisely what corridor it was between Zepa and Srebrenica that you referred to, which at the beginning of 1992 was the route taken by you when you went from Zepa to Srebrenica and Zeleni Jadar? So mark in that corridor -- the direction of the corridor in pencil, and then put a number there.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have to zoom in further. I still can't read the names properly around Zeleni Jadar. I'll try and find where Zeleni Jadar is, but it needs to be zoomed in. Thank you. Let's see what we get when we zoom in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank the technical booth. I think that is sufficient. Now we can see both enclaves, so let's see how they're connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So put a dotted line, please, with your stylus, indicating the corridor between Zepa and Srebrenica which was used by the population to move from one region to the other. So a dotted line, but so we can see the place names, and you can put a number there where there are no place names so that we don't write over them.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't seem to find it in this Srebrenica enclave. I need to find Zeleni Jadar, which is some way off from Skelane.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me help you out. You don't need to show Zeleni Jadar. Just indicate the corridor which went from the Zepa enclave, as it's indicated here, towards the Srebrenica enclave. Just that connecting line. You don't have to go to Zeleni Jadar now. We'll come to that in due course.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try. But whether I'm going to be precise enough, I don't know. I know that it ran along the Drina River, followed the Drina River, approximately like this [marks]. What number do you want me to put there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Put a number 1 in the same colour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm going to remind you of a part of your testimony, and then we can move on to my next question. On page 4255 of the transcript of the 23rd of August, 2010, lines 4 to 6, page 13, you said: "Zepa lies in a valley, and, in the military sense, you can find Zepa fairly easily, as opposed to some other locations." Now, in lines 15 to 19, you said the following: "If we are referring to the entire enclave, then the two enclaves bordered on each other for a time, and you could walk from Srebrenica to Zepa. When I said that you could go from one enclave to another, I mean passing through the villages that were found in the border area between the two enclaves, Srebrenica and Zepa." I think I quoted you properly from the transcript. You can say if I did or didn't.
